profile.name: Naing Htoo Lwin
profile.bio: Software engineering student at the University of Sheffield with a focus on building useful, reliable systems and explaining how they work. Currently working on Android apps, full-stack web applications, and learning to think clearly about engineering trade-offs.
profile.heroHeadline: I build software to understand how things work.
profile.heroStandfirst: I'm Finn, a software engineering student exploring the space between software, AI, and intelligent systems. I like taking ambiguous problems, turning them into working software, and learning from the decisions, failures, and trade-offs along the way.

projects.title: Vigil
projects.deck: A self-hosted, privacy-first web analytics and security monitoring platform that turns raw website traffic into live metrics, bot scores, and a 3D map of where requests come from.
projects.pullQuote: Losing a location is acceptable; losing the page view is not.

numbers.label: target hosting cost, one free-tier VM

projects.figureCaption: Fig. 1 — Request path through Vigil. Intake, enrichment and scoring happen before storage; the dashboard reads aggregates and a live WebSocket feed.

sections.problem: Most analytics tools either send visitor data to a third party, charge a monthly fee, or need serious infrastructure to self-host. For my own sites I wanted to see who was visiting, where they were coming from, and what looked automated, without cookies, fingerprinting, or a bill. I set one hard constraint from the start: the whole system had to run on a single free-tier virtual machine.
sections.investigation: Vigil started in July 2025 as a Python command-line script written during the IEUK 2025 programme. It parsed web server logs with a regular expression, counted requests by IP, endpoint and hour, and flagged user agents that matched common crawler patterns. It could answer questions about a log file after the fact, but it could not say anything about traffic as it happened, and every run started from zero. For the second version I worked out what a real-time system would need: an intake endpoint that stays fast, storage designed for time-bucketed queries, and a dashboard that updates live. TimescaleDB fitted the free-tier constraint because it is a Postgres extension rather than another service to run, while still providing time_bucket queries and continuous aggregates.
sections.implementation: The backend is an asynchronous FastAPI service using SQLAlchemy and Alembic migrations. A small JavaScript snippet, added to a site with one script tag, sends page views to a /collect endpoint, including navigations in single-page apps, with guards against double-loading and duplicate events. Each request is enriched with location data from MaxMind GeoLite2, given a 0-100 bot score by a heuristic engine (user-agent patterns, request rate, missing referrer), and stored in a TimescaleDB hypertable. Metrics endpoints group traffic into buckets from five minutes to one day, and an hourly continuous aggregate pre-computes totals, unique IPs, bot share and p95 latency. The React and TypeScript dashboard includes traffic charts, top pages, IPs and user agents, a WebSocket live tail, JWT authentication with per-site management, and a 3D globe built with React Three Fiber that plots traffic origins sized by volume. The parser from the original script was refactored into the new backend and is covered by unit tests alongside the detection engine.
sections.whatBroke: Several of the hardest problems came from the database layer rather than the application code. TimescaleDB requires the time column in every unique constraint, so the requests table needed a composite primary key of id and timestamp. The asyncpg driver rejected bucket intervals passed as strings, so they are now passed as Python timedelta values. Refreshing a continuous aggregate cannot run inside a transaction, so it could not live in an Alembic migration and is handled by a refresh policy instead. The main trade-off still open is the pipeline itself: /collect currently writes to the database and broadcasts to the live tail within the same request. That keeps the system easy to reason about while it takes shape, but it couples intake to storage. Moving processing behind a Redis Streams worker, so traffic spikes cannot block collection, is the next architectural step. The bot score is also deliberately simple. It catches crawlers that identify themselves, but not bots that disguise their user agent, and request-rate scoring is not yet wired into live ingestion.
sections.outcome: The core flow works end to end in local development with Docker Compose: a site can be registered, the snippet embedded, and page views appear in the dashboard, live tail and globe as they arrive. The remaining roadmap covers the Redis Streams worker, server log forwarding for Nginx and Apache, threshold-based alerting with webhook delivery, production deployment on Oracle Cloud's free tier with the dashboard on Vercel, and a CI/CD pipeline.
sections.learned: Rebuilding a script as a system showed me how much of the work sits between components: schema design, migrations, data types crossing the driver boundary, and deciding where each piece of processing should happen. It also made me more careful about the claims a tool makes. A bot score is only as good as its signals, and writing tests for the heuristics made their blind spots far easier to see than looking at dashboard output.

projects.title: Meeting Cost Calculator
projects.deck: A web application built for an AMRC client to make the cost of meetings easier to understand and manage.
projects.figureCaption: Fig. 1 — The import difference view. Changes are staged and shown before anything is written. Illustrative data.

sections.problem: The project was developed for an AMRC client to help organisations understand the cost of meetings based on participants, roles, grades, and charge-out rates. The application needed to make this information easier to manage while supporting real-world workflow such as importing calendar data and maintaining user and client information.
sections.investigation: Working as part of a six-person software engineering tea, we translated the client's requirements into an application that could support different meeting and organisational workflows. We worked iteratively and used the client's feedback to refine the system throughtout development.
sections.implementation: I worked primarily on the data import and management workflows. This included implementing CSV upload functionality, a preview and difference view before changed were applied, searching and inline editing of grade information, and client email functionality. The application was built using Ruby on Rails with PostgreSQL.
sections.whatBroke: One of the recurring challenges was making data-management workflow safe enought for users to understand before commiting changes. Importing a CSV should not simply overwrite existing information without showing what is going to change. This led to the inclusion of a preview and difference workflow so users could inspect changes first.
sections.outcome: The team delivered a working web application for the AMRC client and achieved a first class result. My contribution focused on several of the application's data-management and client-facing workflows.
sections.learned: The project taught me how mch software engineering happens outside of writing individual features. Working with a real client made requirements, communication, data integrity, and usability feel much more concrete. It also gave me experience contributing to a larger codebase where my work had to fit into decisions made by the rest of the team.

projects.title: SORTS -  Embedded AI Waste Sorting System
projects.deck: An embedded AI waste-sorting prototye combining computer vision, microcontrollers, and physical actuation.
projects.figureCaption: Fig. 1 — The SORTS loop, built in six hours: capture, classify, actuate.

sections.problem: We wanted to explore whether computer vision could be connected to a physical waste-sorting system capable of identifying objects and deciding where they should be placed. The challenge was not just recognising an object, but connecting sensing, inference, and physical actuation into one working system.
sections.investigation: The project was developed during a six-hour multidisciplinary hackathon. We experimented with an ESP32-CAM for image capture, a Python inference pipeline for processing the captured images, and the Gemini API for image classificaton before passing the result into the embedded system.
sections.implementation: I developed the Python-based data processing and inference pipeline and integrated the Google Gemini API to classify waste from captured images. The wider system combined the ESP32-CAM, Arduino Uno R4, and software components into a single embedded prototype.
sections.whatBroke: The biggest challenge was connecting an AI model to a physical system. A classification result that looks reasonable on a screen still needs to be translated into a reliable action by hardware. Camera positioning, real-world objects, communication between components, and the limitations of a short hackthon all affected the system.
sections.outcome: We delivered a functional embedded waste-sorting prototype within six hours and received the Most Adventurous Hack award at iForge Hack Day 2025.
sections.learned: SORTS was one of my first experiences working across software, AI, and physical hardware. It taught me to think about intelligent systems as complete pipelines rather than isolated models and showed me how quickly real-world constraints appear once software has to control something physical.

philosophy.principle: Start with the constraint, not the framework.
philosophy.position: Understanding the real limitation shapes every decision that follows. Choosing a tool before understanding the constraint is backwards.
philosophy.example: Vigil had one hard constraint: it had to run on a single free-tier virtual machine. That ruled out running a separate time-series database and led me to TimescaleDB, which runs inside Postgres but still provides time-bucketed queries and continuous aggregates. The constraint chose the tool, not the other way round.

philosophy.position: Every engineering decision is a trade-off. The job is to make those trade-offs explicit so collaborators, and users, can challenge them.
philosophy.example: On the Meeting Cost Calculator, a CSV import could silently overwrite the grade and rate data behind every cost figure. Instead of hiding that risk, the import shows a preview and a difference view first, so the person making the change can see exactly what will happen before deciding.

philosophy.principle: Build the smallest reliable version first.
philosophy.position: A working small thing teaches more than a broken ambitious one. Reliability compounds.
philosophy.example: SORTS had six hours. We focused on one complete loop, capture an image, classify it, move the hardware, before adding anything else. A narrow pipeline that worked end to end was worth more than a clever model with nothing attached to it.

philosophy.principle: Treat failure modes as part of the design.
philosophy.position: What happens when a dependency is missing, slow or wrong is a design question, not a clean-up task for later.
philosophy.example: Vigil's location lookup skips private and loopback addresses, and if the GeoIP database is missing or a lookup fails, it returns nothing rather than failing the request. Losing a location is acceptable; losing the page view is not.

philosophy.principle: Validate the direction before building all of it.
philosophy.position: A brief, a sketch or a static mockup can reject a bad idea in an afternoon. Building it fully can take weeks.
philosophy.example: I built one portfolio design through six full phases before admitting it did not work. For this version I wrote a design brief and settled the typography, palette and structure before writing a single component.

fieldNotes.title: Three portfolio designs I built and threw away
fieldNotes.body:
This site is the fourth design direction I have tried for my portfolio. I built most of two of the others before deciding they were wrong. That was expensive, but it taught me more about design process than anything that worked first time.

## 1. Render

The first direction was a 3D hero: a lo-fi workspace scene built with React Three Fiber, meant to feel like sitting down at my desk. I got it running, but procedural geometry has a quality ceiling. Without properly modelled assets the scene never looked as good as the idea in my head, and writing more code did not close that gap.

## 2. Newspaper × Code

Next was a hybrid of editorial layout and developer culture: a newspaper grid, Playfair Display headlines, warm grey paper, and commit messages as section labels. I built it fully, across six phases. By the end it worked, but it felt like two concepts competing for attention rather than one clear identity.

## 3. Doodle Notebook

The third idea was a hand-drawn notebook, with sketchy illustrations on lined paper. This time I stopped at the concept stage. When I pictured a recruiter skimming it on a laptop between meetings, the charm did not outweigh the effort it would take to read.

## 4. The Engineering Edition

The current design keeps the editorial part that worked and drops the gimmicks: Source Serif 4 and Inter, cream paper and charcoal ink, restrained motion, and projects written as case studies rather than cards.

## What I would tell myself earlier

- **Validate a direction before building it.** A written brief and a few static mockups would have caught the problems with the second direction in an afternoon, not six phases.
- **Know where the ceiling is.** Some ideas are limited by assets or skills you do not have yet, not by effort.
- **Separate content from presentation.** This version reads everything from one structured content source. If there is ever a fifth design, it will be a new front end rather than a rewrite of everything.

fieldNotes.title: Three TimescaleDB gotchas I hit in one week
fieldNotes.body:
Vigil stores every request in a TimescaleDB hypertable. TimescaleDB is a Postgres extension, which is exactly why I chose it: one database to run on a free-tier VM, with time-series features on top. Most of it behaved like ordinary Postgres. Three things did not.

## 1. The primary key has to include the time column

A hypertable is split into chunks by time. For a unique constraint to be enforced across all of those chunks, the partitioning column has to be part of it. My first model used a plain auto-incrementing `id` as the primary key, and turning the table into a hypertable failed.

The fix was a composite primary key of `id` and `timestamp`. It looks unusual in a model definition, but it reflects how the data is actually stored.

## 2. Intervals are not strings

The metrics endpoint groups requests with `time_bucket()`, and the client chooses the bucket size: five minutes, fifteen minutes, an hour or a day. I passed the interval as a string like `'1 hour'`, which is what you would type in psql. Through asyncpg it failed, because the driver infers the parameter type as `text`, not `interval`.

asyncpg maps a Python `timedelta` to a Postgres `INTERVAL` natively, so the fix was a small lookup table from bucket names to `timedelta` values. A side benefit: an unexpected bucket name now falls back to a known value instead of reaching the query.

## 3. Some commands cannot run in a migration

Vigil keeps an hourly continuous aggregate, a materialised view of totals, unique IPs, bot share and p95 latency that TimescaleDB keeps up to date. I wanted the migration to create the view and fill it straight away. But `refresh_continuous_aggregate()` cannot run inside a transaction block, and Alembic runs each migration inside one.

The migration now creates the view `WITH NO DATA` and adds a refresh policy. The policy fills it on its first scheduled run and re-processes the last few hours each time, so late-arriving data is still counted.

## The common thread

None of these were bugs in my application logic. Each was a place where an assumption from plain Postgres did not survive contact with the extension or the driver. Reading the error carefully, then reading the documentation for the layer that produced it, was faster every time than changing code and hoping.

fieldNotes.title: From a log script to a live pipeline: where Vigil came from
fieldNotes.body:
Vigil started as a single Python file. During the IEUK 2025 programme I was given a web server log and asked to work out what was happening in it: who was sending the most traffic, which endpoints were busiest, and whether any of it looked automated.

## The first version

The script read the log line by line, matched each line against one regular expression, and counted things: requests per IP, hits per endpoint, traffic per hour. Any user agent containing words like `bot`, `crawl`, `spider`, `python` or `curl` was flagged as suspicious. It printed a summary and exited.

It worked, and it was useful for the task. But it had three limits that became obvious as soon as I imagined running it on my own sites:

- **It only worked after the fact.** You needed a finished log file before you could learn anything.
- **Every run started from zero.** Nothing was stored, so there was no history to compare against.
- **Detection was yes or no.** A user agent either matched the pattern or it did not.

## What changed in v2

Each limit became a design decision.

To see traffic as it happens, v2 collects page views from a small JavaScript snippet and streams them to the dashboard over a WebSocket. To keep history, requests go into a TimescaleDB hypertable, where time-bucketed queries stay fast as the table grows. And instead of yes or no, each request gets a bot score from 0 to 100 built from several signals, so where to draw the line is a decision rather than something baked into a regex.

## What survived

The original parsing regex is still in the codebase, refactored into the backend's parser service and now covered by tests. The crawler pattern from the first script is the first signal in the new scoring engine. The legacy script is kept in the repository too, partly for history and partly as a reminder that a working small tool is a good place to start.

## What is next

Ingestion currently writes straight to the database inside the request. The next step is a Redis Streams worker between intake and storage, so a burst of traffic cannot slow down collection.

fieldNotes.title: Why the CSV import shows you a diff first
fieldNotes.body:
On Software Hut, my team built a Meeting Cost Calculator for a client at the AMRC. The application works out what a meeting costs from who attends, their grade, and the charge-out rate for that grade. I worked mainly on the data import and management side, including CSV upload.

## The obvious version

The simplest way to build an import is: upload a file, parse it, write every row to the database. It is quick to build and easy to demo.

The problem is what the data does. Grades and rates feed directly into every cost the application shows. A file with one wrong column, an old export or a changed rate could quietly shift figures across the whole system, and the person uploading it would have no way of knowing until someone noticed a strange number.

## The version we shipped

Instead of applying changes straight away, the import works in stages:

1. **Upload.** The file is parsed and checked, but nothing is saved.
2. **Preview.** The user sees what the file contains.
3. **Difference view.** Rows are compared against existing data, so new, changed and unchanged records are shown separately.
4. **Confirm.** Only then are changes written.

The same idea shaped the grades page. Edits are staged and saved together rather than saved instantly on every change, because accidental instant saves are a poor fit for data that affects money.

## The trade-off

This took more work to build and test, and it adds a step for the user. For a file with no real changes it can feel slower than it needs to be. But the cost of the extra step is a few seconds, and the cost of a silent mistake is a figure nobody trusts afterwards.

## What I took from it

The question I now ask about any feature that changes data is: *can the user see what is about to happen before it happens?* If the answer is no, and the data matters, that is usually worth fixing before anything else.
